raw_case_text:
A 58-year old male was referred to our outpatient consultation centre with complaints of shortness of breath, dry cough and fatigue over the previous two months. He also reported anorexia and involuntary weight loss for the same period of time. His primary care physician had treated him with antibiotics, but no response or improvement in symptoms were noted. The patient's past medical history included an episode of pesticide poisoning 35 years ago for which no information was available and occasional gout that responded to anti-inflammatory medication. The patient was an ex-smoker of 80-pack years and a moderate drinker. No known allergies were reported. His occupational history included working as a stacker in a warehouse for 20 years, with moderate dust exposure, and following this, as an administrative worker for 20 years. He was regularly exposed to a parakeet (Melopsittacus undulatus), chickens, and cats. The patient was unaware of any exposure to tuberculosis patients, recent trips abroad or family history of respiratory disease.
On physical examination, he was in good general condition, but crackles were heard in both lung bases. No other changes were noted.
The patient's chest X-ray showed bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates with a predominant reticular pattern and no spared areas (Figure 1). This was followed by a high resolution computed tomography (HRCT) scan of the chest that showed several areas of subpleural cystic lesions and traction bronchiectasis affecting all lobes, but having an upper and middle level predominance and being much more extensive in the right lung. There were also multiple mediastinal enlarged lymph nodes and an enlargement of the pulmonary artery (3.2 cm diameter) and right cardiac cavities (Figure 2). Cardiac tests were performed, including an electrocardiogram and echocardiogram, and no other signs of cardiac disease were found. Blood tests, including those for auto-antibodies and IgG immunoglobulins (to parakeet and fungal proteins) were negative. Lung function tests suggested moderate restriction (percentage predicted forced vital capacity [FVC], 57.5%), low diffusion capacity ([DLco] 36% of the predicted value) and resting hypoxaemia (PaO2, 69.7 mmHg). The decision was made to perform bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy. Upon examination, the bronchial mucosa showed moderate signs of inflammation, but no other morphological changes. Bronchoalveolar lavage showed an increase in the total cell count (300 cells/microL), and increased percentage of lymphocytes (28%) and neutrophils (12%). The CD4/CD8 ratio was 0.2. Transbronchial biopsy showed no specific findings. A transthoracic biopsy was then performed, but the results were also inconclusive. The patient was referred for surgical lung biopsy. The pathology of the surgical specimen was compatible with a pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia (Figure 3).
At this time no definite diagnosis could be made, as the clinical, radiological and pathological findings were compatible with both chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis and IPF. Nevertheless, treatment with prednisolone, azathioprine and acetylcysteine commenced. The patient was also instructed to avoid any contact with the parakeet. Despite the treatment, the patient got progressively worse, and has been referred for lung transplantation.
Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis and IPF can present with the same clinical and radiological manifestations. A careful clinical evaluation is therefore fundamental, and the surgical pulmonary biopsy is usually helpful in performing the differential diagnosis, but not in this case. A UIP pattern can be seen on biopsy (and/or CT) in both IPF and chronic HP. The addition of BAL can give a decisive contribution to the diagnostic procedures. A cut-off level of 30% for lymphocytes in BAL demonstrated a favorable discriminative power for the diagnosis of IPF. In this case, despite careful evaluation, no definite diagnosis could be achieved.
Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying images. A copy of the written consent is available for review by the Editor of this journal.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 58-year-old male ex-smoker presented with a 2-month history of progressive shortness of breath, dry cough, fatigue, anorexia, and involuntary weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 2 months prior to outpatient referral, the patient developed progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, fatigue, anorexia, and weight loss that failed to improve with primary care antibiotic therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: 80-pack-year ex-smoker, moderate alcohol drinker; history of pesticide poisoning 35 years prior and occasional gout. Worked for 20 years as a warehouse stacker (moderate dust exposure) and 20 years in administration; regular domestic exposure to a parakeet (Melopsittacus undulatus), chickens, and cats. No known TB contact, recent travel, drug allergies, or family history of lung disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dyspnea, dry cough, fatigue, anorexia, and weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Good general condition; bilateral basal Velcro-like crackles on lung auscultation; otherwise unremarkable exam.
objective.routine_investigations: Negative autoantibodies and negative serum specific IgG precipitins to parakeet and fungal antigens. ECG and echocardiogram were normal. Pulmonary function tests showed moderate restriction (FVC 57.5% predicted), severely reduced diffusing capacity (DLCO 36% predicted), and resting hypoxemia (PaO2 69.7 mmHg). Chest X-ray showed diffuse bilateral reticular interstitial infiltrates.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest HRCT demonstrated diffuse subpleural cystic honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis across all lobes (predominantly right lung and upper/middle zones), enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, main pulmonary artery dilatation (3.2 cm), and right heart chamber enlargement. Bronchoscopy showed mild mucosal inflammation; BAL revealed 300 cells/µL with 28% lymphocytes, 12% neutrophils, and a CD4/CD8 ratio of 0.2. Transbronchial and transthoracic needle biopsies were inconclusive, and surgical lung biopsy demonstrated a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) histopathological pattern.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Infectious etiologies including tuberculosis were excluded, and based on HRCT, BAL lymphocytosis (28%), and surgical lung biopsy showing a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern, the differential narrowed to chronic bird-fancier's hypersensitivity pneumonitis versus idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Despite avian antigen avoidance and therapy with prednisolone, azathioprine, and N-acetylcysteine, his respiratory status progressively worsened and he was referred for lung transplantation.
